item.title: MMR overtakes NCR as India’s biggest housing market: Mumbai region takes 26% share
item.description: MMR has surpassed NCR as India's largest housing market by sales value in H1 2026, driven by volume growth.
item.content:encoded:
MMR overtakes NCR as India’s biggest housing market: Mumbai region takes 26% share
India’s housing market saw a clear shift in H1 2026, with Mumbai Metropolitan Region emerging as the largest market by sales value. While MMR benefited from stronger volumes, NCR saw a sharp correction in sales, particularly across its premium and luxury housing segments.
Mumbai Metropolitan Region (MMR) has emerged as India’s largest Tier-1 housing market, overtaking the National Capital Region (NCR) in terms of primary housing sales value in the first half of 2026, according to the India Housing Report by NAR and CRE Matrix.
MMR accounted for 26% of primary housing sales value across Tier-1 cities in H1 2026, compared with 19% for NCR. The Mumbai region recorded housing sales worth around ₹93,800 crore, up 8% from a year earlier, with sales volumes rising around 9%.
The shift comes as the broader Indian housing market enters a period of slower growth. Across Tier-1 cities, primary housing sales were worth around ₹3.63 lakh crore in H1 2026, broadly unchanged from the record level seen in H1 2025. Volumes, however, declined around 2% to approximately 2.58 lakh units.
MMR growth gets a volume boost
The MMR market was supported by stronger sales activity across several locations. In Mumbai, primary housing sales value increased around 4% to ₹58,362 crore, while volumes remained broadly flat at around 24,500 units.
The average ticket size in Mumbai rose 4% to a record ₹2.38 crore, making price growth the main contributor to the increase in sales value. Homes priced at ₹5 crore and above accounted for around 40% of sales value, up from 38% a year earlier.
MUST READ: Mumbai prime home prices rise 6.2% in Q2 2026, ranks 8th globally: Knight Frank
Outside Mumbai, Navi Mumbai and Raigad stood out as a major growth engine. Sales value in the region jumped around 29% to ₹12,292 crore in H1 2026. Volumes increased 20% to approximately 17,300 units, while the average ticket size rose 8% to ₹71 lakh. New launches also surged 29% to around 25,800 units.
NCR loses ground
NCR's housing market moved in the opposite direction. Primary housing sales value declined 24% to ₹68,217 crore in H1 2026, while volumes fell around 9% to 24,600 units.
The average ticket size also dropped 16% to ₹2.77 crore, from ₹3.31 crore in H1 2025. At the same time, developers launched around 35,000 units, up 10% and the highest half-year level in the report's series.

Gurugram accounted for a significant part of the correction. Sales value there fell around 33% to ₹37,726 crore, even as volumes remained broadly stable at about 12,000 units. The average ticket size fell 32% to ₹3.15 crore from its H1 2025 peak of ₹4.65 crore.

The luxury segment also lost some share in Gurugram. Homes priced at ₹5 crore and above accounted for 52% of sales value, down from 66% in H1 2025, while the ₹2-5 crore segment increased its share.
The report also highlights that housing supply is picking up faster than absorption nationally. Developers launched around 2.98 lakh units in H1 2026, up 7% year-on-year, while the average ticket size was broadly stable at ₹1.41 crore.
With sales value no longer accelerating despite higher supply, the report suggests that the next phase of housing growth will depend increasingly on actual volume absorption and end-user demand, rather than continued price escalation.

item.title: AI safety requires eyes inside the lab
item.description: An Anthropic executive proposes embedded evaluation and international coordination to govern AI development and ensure safety.
item.content:encoded:
'In a race toward systems whose controllability has not been demonstrated, being first...may simply mean losing control first.'
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has called on companies and governments to “pace the frontier”: AI capabilities should not advance faster than safeguards. Anthropic has committed to giving independent evaluators ongoing, employee-like access to its laboratories.
His proposal raises a fundamental question: How can public authorities govern a technology when most relevant knowledge remains inside private companies? Embedded evaluation is the first step in his three-part plan, followed by coordination among democracies and then global coordination. The OpenAI-Hugging Face incident illustrates the problem. During a cybersecurity evaluation, agents meant to operate separately found an unauthorized communication channel.
According to one of the few AI evaluation organizations, METR, roughly 1,200 agents exchanged over 70,000 messages and files, and about 700 participated in attacks on AI platform Hugging Face. Some recognized that the activity exceeded their assigned tasks but continued because it might help satisfy the evaluation objective. The incident showed that agents pursuing an objective can combine capabilities, tools and opportunities in unanticipated ways. Mature safety-critical sectors have public systems of certification, inspection, investigation and enforcement.
U.S. automakers self-certify compliance, but government sets standards, investigates defects and can require recalls. Frontier AI lacks a comparable system of continuous public oversight. This points to a paradox: one of the most powerful technologies humans have designed currently has among the least public oversight of any comparable industry. Two characteristics complicate oversight.
Even with unchanged weights, a model’s behavior can change with prompts, tools, memory, permissions, other agents and its environment. Fine-tuning changes the model itself or recursive self-improvement rewrites it.
Meanwhile, private companies develop and operate the leading models, control computing infrastructure and employ the technical teams. Governments may establish binding rules for companies developing and deploying AI models while still lacking timely visibility into those companies’ development processes. Governments should seize upon Anthropic’s commitment as a pilot project to bridge the chasm between industry and public knowledge regarding frontier AI models. Embedded supervision would bring technical knowledge into public decision-making.
Industry retains operational and legal responsibility, while public institutions determine acceptable societal risk. Without knowledge, public authority remains largely formal or relies on information too coarse to support timely decisions. Companies can delay unsafe models, just as carmakers can withhold vehicles with faulty brakes. But a company cannot bind competitors, independently verify its own restraint or determine what catastrophic risks society should accept.
This is a legitimate government decision. If it is left to a company, political power passes to someone who was never voted for. Supervision must preserve corporate responsibility. Incumbents might exploit complex rules to obstruct competitors or obscure liability.
Supervisors therefore need public accreditation, protection from retaliatory dismissal, access to models, logs, training and evaluation environments, and incident data and reporting rights without corporate veto. Rotation, conflict-of-interest rules and confidentiality protections are essential. Relevant access should extend to safety cases and emerging alignment failures. Evaluators also need defined escalation rights: requiring additional testing, notifying authorities, recommending restrictions and initiating a legally reviewable pause when agreed thresholds are crossed.
Embedded supervision is not itself control. It supplies information for accountability and timely intervention. Technical standards can define evaluation methods, reporting requirements and security practices. They cannot guarantee that successor models will not exhibit misaligned behavior or new failure modes, or overcome incentives to accelerate.
The EU AI Act provides substantive obligations and intervention powers. Providers of general purpose models with systemic risk face evaluation, mitigation, incident reporting and cybersecurity requirements. The European Commission can request information, evaluate models, demand mitigation, impose fines and require withdrawal or recall. Yet legal authority needs timely, continuously updated technical knowledge.
The EU AI Office moved early: early September, it sent its first formal requests for information to more than 30 relevant providers, while the Code of Practice contemplates involvement by the Office and third parties throughout the model life cycle when necessary. California has begun exploring a similar approach through Governor Newsom’s recent executive order. The EU mechanisms provide a foundation for oversight, although it does not establish permanent independent supervision inside every frontier laboratory.
President Donald Trump’s June 2, 2026 executive order directs agencies to design a voluntary framework offering federal access to covered frontier models for up to 30 days before release to other trusted partners. Its early access section does not authorize mandatory licensing or preclearance. This cybersecurity-focused approach can reveal risks, but a testing window cannot substitute for life cycle supervision: new failure modes may emerge with fine-tuning, tools, longer operation or interaction with other agents.
In frontier model development, commercial and strategic competition share much of the same industrial base. A broad slowdown in developing more powerful models therefore delays the new strategic capabilities that depend on them. A serious incident in a democracy could provoke social and political repercussions severe enough to trigger a domestic pause in frontier model development, slowing the associated advance in strategic capabilities. Integrated oversight could help us advance as quickly as our safeguards can reliably support.
In Italy, we say, “Those who go slowly go safely and far. ” In a race toward systems whose controllability has not been demonstrated, being first to the frontier may not mean winning. It may simply mean losing control first. Roberto Baldoni is former deputy director general of Italian Intelligence and the founding director general of the National Cybersecurity Agency .
He is currently senior adviser for technology and cybersecurity policy to the Italian ambassador to the United States, and honorary professor of computer science at Sapienza University of Rome. The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not reflect the official position of the Italian government.

item.title: American-Made Must Mean Mission-Ready
item.description: An article discusses the importance of balancing "Buy American" policies with the necessity of providing service members with mission-ready equipment, following boot failures in Norway.
item.content:encoded:
American service members should have the best equipment available for the mission they are being asked to perform.
After 24 years of military service as a decorated Army officer and Iraq War veteran, an Air Force Reserve commander, and now serving in emergency management with Joint Task Force–National Capital Region, I’ve learned that equipment is only as good as its ability to perform under real-world conditions.
In the Arctic, a failed boot is not just an inconvenience. It can become a safety issue and potentially an operational readiness problem. That’s why the recent Newsweek report of Marines experiencing boot failures during cold-weather training in Norway deserves serious attention. Marines training ahead of NATO’s Cold Response 2026 exercise reported holes forming in their boots, soles separating, and freezing water getting inside.
Some Marines had to be pulled from training, and post-exercise inspection found hundreds of additional deficiencies in the same model of cold-weather boot. While a strong domestic defense industrial base is an important national security asset, we don’t want to find ourselves in a major conflict unable to produce the uniforms, footwear and equipment our service members need because critical manufacturing capacity has moved overseas.
Supporters of the BOOTS Act make exactly that argument: relying too heavily on foreign suppliers creates vulnerabilities of its own. But there’s another side of readiness that is non-negotiable. The equipment has to work to protect the safety of our troops. During my military career, I’ve learned that conditions thousands miles away on the ground almost never match the plans made at home.
Commanders need to be able to respond to the environment in front of them, especially when the health and safety of their service members are at stake. That’s exactly what happened in Norway. When American cold-weather boots failed, U.S. forces used an established Host Nation Support mechanism to obtain locally available footwear. Marines were able to continue training with equipment suited to the conditions rather than waiting for another shipment from the United States.
That’s not a failure of American readiness. Flexibility is part of our readiness. Norway has spent generations preparing its military to operate in extreme cold. The Norwegian M77 boots obtained for some Marines were developed with the Norwegian military decades ago for their environment.
If one of our NATO allies has proven equipment designed for a specific environment, commanders should have an appropriate pathway to use it when American equipment cannot meet the immediate operational requirement. The debate over the BOOTS Act brings that question into sharper focus. The legislation would require optional combat boots worn by U.S. service members to be entirely manufactured in the United States using American-sourced materials.
Its supporters argue that doing so would strengthen domestic manufacturing, reduce dependence on foreign supply chains and ensure the United States has the industrial capacity to supply its military during a major conflict. The experience in Norway shows why sourcing requirements and performance requirements have to work together. We should, without a doubt, invest in American manufacturers. We should build the domestic capacity to produce the best military equipment in the world.
We should have rigorous standards for durability, safety and performance, particularly for equipment designed for extreme environments. America should always strive to have the best equipment and set the highest standards. At the same time, we should preserve enough operational flexibility to recognize that no single supply chain can anticipate every battlefield, climate or mission. Congress has already recognized the importance of performance.
Current law requires the military services to establish combat-boot quality assurance processes addressing durability, quality, specialty-specific operating environments and biomechanics. American service members should have the best equipment available for the mission they are being asked to perform. If American manufacturers can provide it, we should be proud to put American-made boots on American troops.
If domestic capacity or equipment falls short in a specialized environment, commanders should have a clear and accountable way to obtain proven equipment from trusted allies until that gap is fixed at home. We ask our service members to operate in deserts, mountains, jungles and Arctic cold. We ask them to deploy around the world, often with little notice, and perform under conditions most Americans will never experience.
They should never have to wonder whether the boots on their feet can survive the mission. Buy American should strengthen military readiness, but it should never come at readiness’s expense. Dr. Josh McConkey is a US Air Force Reserve Colonel, Army combat veteran, emergency physician and candidate for Lieutenant Governor of North Carolina. The views expressed in this article are the writer's own.

item.title: RBI Dy. Governor lists 5 growth areas for NBFC sector amid new challenges and opportunities
item.description: An RBI Deputy Governor outlined five key areas for the sustainable growth of India's Non-Banking Financial Companies (NBFC) sector.
item.content:encoded:
As the role of NBFCs changes from alternative lenders to specialised financial partners, RBI Deputy Governor Shirish Chandra Murmu has shared five areas that matter most for sustainable growth as the sector faces new challenges alongside new opportunities.
NBFC credit today is about 16.7 per cent of nominal GDP, up from 15.9 per cent a year earlier. It is about 27 per cent of the credit extended by Scheduled Commercial Banks, up from 26 per cent.
In the latest RBI Bulletin for September, Murmu set out five areas for the NBFC and HFC sector.
“Good governance is the foundation of every strong institution. Boards and senior management must build a culture of sustained compliance and ethics across the organisation. As the sector scales, that strength must scale with it,” he suggested.
The second area is liquidity management. Past liquidity events have shown how exposed NBFCs and HFCs can be to shifts in market sentiment and funding concentration.
“Strong liquidity risk management is not optional. Recent episodes in some advanced economies are reminder of this. Entities must diversify their funding sources. A deep, liquid corporate bond market will help, and we will keep working with market participants to build one,” he wrote.
Securitisation should also grow beyond a liquidity tool – into a genuine way to transfer risk and free up capital, with proper skin-in-the-game and transparency rules, Murmu added.
Third, as credit growth speeds up, so does the risk to asset quality. Lenders need rigorous stress testing, early-warning systems, and dynamic provisioning. AI and machine learning tools should be used more to detect early signs of borrower stress.
“Let me be clear: growth must never come at the cost of underwriting standards,” he mentioned.
Fourth, customer trust is fundamental to sustainable business, and the pace of innovation must never outpace the protection, especially of vulnerable customers.
“Conduct regulation, grievance redressal, and responsible lending remain top priorities for us. Our recent guidelines on conduct of recovery agent reflect this priority. In an age where feedback travels instantly, there is no substitute for public trust,” said Murmu.
The last area is digital transformation and cyber resilience. Technology adoption must keep deepening – from blockchain in supply chain finance to AI in fraud detection.
“But digitalisation brings cyber risk. Cyber resilience must stay a top priority. Entities must invest in strong cyber security to protect customer data and maintain trust. Innovation must serve both efficiency and fairness,” Murmu stressed.

item.title: African Expansion: Nigerian Banks Face Tougher Regulatory Rules, Analysts Warn
item.description: Analysts warn Nigerian banks expanding across Africa must deepen compliance and develop local talent due to tightening regulatory rules in host countries.
item.content:encoded:
Analysts say Nigerian banks expanding across Africa must deepen compliance and develop local talent as regulators tighten market rules.
Analysts have urged Nigerian banks operating across Africa as well as those planning further expansion on the continent, to deepen compliance with host-country regulations as African regulators tighten rules governing foreign-owned financial institutions.
The warning comes as The Gambia recently directed commercial banks to begin phasing out non-Gambian employees.
Also, during the week, Kenya approved the transfer of the business, assets and liabilities of Access Bank Kenya to National Bank of Kenya (NBK), paving the way for the integration of the two entities.
Although the developments are different in nature, analysts said they underscore the increasingly complex regulatory environment Nigerian banks must navigate as they expand across African markets.
The developments also highlight the need for lenders to adopt market-specific strategies, strengthen local compliance and invest in indigenous talent rather than relying on a uniform approach to continental expansion.
In The Gambia, the Central Bank of The Gambia (CBG) directed commercial banks operating in the country, including subsidiaries of Nigerian lenders Access Bank, FirstBank, GTBank and Zenith Bank, to commence a phased replacement of non-Gambian employees with suitably qualified Gambian nationals.
Speaking with THISDAY, Director, Deals Advisory, PwC Nigeria, Wale Olusi, said the directive did not prevent foreign-owned banks from operating in The Gambia but required them to comply with the country’s regulations.
“On the Gambia, the regulation clearly doesn’t stop foreign-owned entities or banks from operating, as the case may be, but they must comply with local laws,” Olusi said.
He noted that The Gambia, with a population of about two million, has faced manpower constraints, which have historically resulted in Nigerians and other foreigners occupying senior positions in some institutions.
“The Gambia has a manpower challenge. In fact, a number of Nigerians occupy top positions there precisely because of this gap,” he said.
According to Olusi, the directive was aimed at protecting employment opportunities for Gambians, making it necessary for affected banks to invest more in training and developing local talent.
“What this simply means is that these institutions have to invest in training and empowering locals, building their capacity to do the jobs required, if they wish to continue operating in The Gambia,” he said.
He, however, said the development should be viewed within a broader global trend towards greater protection of local employment, noting that similar concerns had emerged in other African countries and developed economies.
“However, if you put what has happened in The Gambia together with what we’ve seen in South Africa and perhaps a few other African countries, there is a growing concern – not just in Africa, but globally – about migrants or expatriates dominating the job market while locals remain unemployed,” he said.
Olusi said the challenge for governments was to ensure that policies aimed at protecting local employment were matched with investment in human capital, enabling local workers to eventually take up positions occupied by expatriates.
Access Bank Gambia has four Gambians out of seven positions reviewed, representing 57.1 per cent, alongside two Nigerians and one Ghanaian. GTBank Gambia has the highest Gambian representation, with five of seven positions, or 71.4 per cent, held by Gambians, while two are Nigerians.
Zenith Bank Gambia has an even split, with three Gambians and three Nigerians among six positions reviewed, giving each nationality 50 per cent representation.
At FirstBank Gambia, Nigerians occupy three of five positions reviewed, representing 60 per cent, while two are Gambian. Ecobank Gambia, which is not Nigerian-owned, has three Gambians, three Ghanaians and one Nigerian among seven positions reviewed, representing 42.9 per cent, 42.9 per cent and 14.3 per cent, respectively.
The figures cover only publicly identifiable board and senior management positions and do not represent the nationality composition of the banks’ entire workforce.
The varying composition suggests that the impact of the Gambian directive could differ across institutions, depending on the extent of expatriate participation in their workforce and senior management.
In his contribution on the matter, Head of Financial Institutions Ratings at Agusto & Co., Ayokunle Olubunmi, said banks should first establish the actual proportion of expatriates occupying senior positions before assessing the directive’s potential impact on their operations.
“We need to establish what proportion of senior management roles are actually occupied by expatriates. It could be very small. It could be just a few banks that have expatriates in those particular positions,” he said.
Olubunmi noted that the push for greater local participation was not peculiar to The Gambia, saying regulators across African markets had increasingly introduced measures to promote indigenous participation in their financial sectors.
“For instance, in Ghana, if a financial institution is foreign-owned, your managing director and chairman cannot both be foreigners. Either the MD or the chairman can be a foreigner,” he added.
He said international banks would need to increasingly develop local executives capable of managing their operations as part of their long-term expansion strategy.
“The truth is that, for most banks that operate internationally, if you really want to penetrate and grow your market share in a particular market, the best way to operate is to ensure that the business is increasingly handled by locals,” Olubunmi said.
The regulatory development in The Gambia came same week Kenya approved the transfer of Access Bank Kenya’s business, assets and liabilities to National Bank of Kenya.
However, Olubunmi stressed that the Central Bank of Kenya did not force Access Bank to merge the two institutions.
He explained: “To correct an impression, the Central Bank of Kenya did not force Access Bank to merge with National Bank of Kenya. They did not.”
According to him, Access Bank already owned both institutions following its acquisition of NBK and had previously announced plans to integrate them.
“Access Bank owns both entities. Access Bank acquired NBK,” he said.
He explained further that NBK had a stronger franchise in Kenya than Access Bank Kenya, making the consolidation part of Access Bank’s strategy to streamline its operations in the market.
He added that the integration was not a new development, as Access Bank had been working towards securing the necessary regulatory approvals.
“If you have been following Access Bank’s conference calls, you would know that they have already mentioned that they were going to merge both entities,” he said.
The development, he said, should therefore not be interpreted as a regulatory directive compelling Access Bank to consolidate its Kenyan operations, but as part of the group’s previously announced strategy.
Olubunmi said the contrasting developments in The Gambia and Kenya nonetheless illustrated the different regulatory and operating considerations Nigerian banks must contend with across African markets.
He stressed that Nigerian banks should not approach continental expansion with a one-size-fits-all strategy, as the regulatory, labour and competitive environments vary from one market to another.
According to him, banks entering smaller African markets could initially deploy executives familiar with their corporate culture and systems while deliberately developing qualified local professionals to take over key responsibilities over time.
“You can have a five- or seven-year strategy where you initially go in with people who understand your culture and operations, and then gradually identify reputable and qualified Gambians who can take over those roles,” he said.
He also pointed to the commercial advantage of employing local executives, particularly for banks seeking to expand their retail and small and medium-sized enterprise businesses.
He added that local executives could better understand the culture and language of the market while combining that knowledge with the bank’s corporate culture.
“So, I don’t think it will discourage expansion if the business case is there. What it will do is affect your strategy,” he said.

item.title: Govt forms high-level panel to fast-track Matarbari projects
item.description: Bangladesh has formed a high-level committee to accelerate the implementation of nine priority projects under the Maheshkhali Integrated Development Authority.
item.content:encoded:
The government has formed a high-level coordination committee to expedite land acquisition, compensation, rehabilitation, and implementation activities for nine priority projects under the Maheshkhali Integrated Development Authority (MIDA), targeted for completion by 2029.
The initiative follows the implementation of the MIDA ordinance which came into effect on August 1, 2025.
MIDA acts as a single administrative body overseeing energy, port expansion, township, logistics, and seven economic zones on Maheshkhali, which already hosts a 1,200 MW power plant and LNG terminals.
Building on that framework, the Prime Minister's Office issued a notification on September 14, establishing the new committee.
According to the notification, the principal secretary to the prime minister will chair the committee, with secretaries of the land, finance, planning, shipping, and power divisions serving as members.
The committee will provide necessary time frames and directions to accelerate land acquisition, compensation for affected people, rehabilitation of displaced populations, and skills and livelihood restoration under MIDA's jurisdiction and adjoining areas.
The nine priority projects include the Matarbari sea port construction (Chittagong Port Authority and Roads and Highways Department portions), a land-based LNG terminal, a land-based LPG terminal and storage facility, and a third floating storage regasification unit.
The list also features the third and fourth coal-based power plants under Coal Power Generation Company Bangladesh, an oil refinery and petrochemical complex, a dockyard/shipyard, and the MIDA office.

item.title: Why 4 in 10 Gen Z workers could struggle in retirement
item.description: A study suggests 42% of Gen Z workers face retirement poverty due to minimum auto-enrolment contributions, prioritizing immediate financial pressures over long-term savings.
item.content:encoded:
Why 4 in 10 Gen Z workers could struggle in retirement
More than two-fifths of Gen Z workers are on track for retirement poverty if they remain at minimum auto-enrolment contribution levels, as younger savers balance pensions against housing and other financial pressures.
Gen Z workers are balancing retirement saving with immediate financial priorities such as housing and the cost of living
By Teena JoseSep 26, 2026
Teena Jose
Teena Jose is a business journalist at Eastern Eye specialising in British Asian business and the UK property market. She reports on market trends, economic developments and business leaders, while also producing daily digital video content on business and finance.
* 42 per cent of Gen Z workers could face retirement poverty at minimum auto-enrolment levels. * Younger savers are prioritising flexible options such as cash savings and ISAs. * Pensions dashboards could make retirement savings easier to track.
For a generation that says it wants financial freedom and the option to retire earlier, saving enough for retirement is becoming a difficult balancing act.
More than two-fifths, or 42 per cent, of Gen Z workers are on track for retirementpoverty if they remain at the minimum auto-enrolment contribution level of 8 per cent of qualifying earnings, according to research from workplace pension provider Penfold.

The finding highlights a growing gap between what younger workers want from their financial future and where their savings are currently heading.
Retirement is competing with more immediate goals
For many younger workers, putting more money into a pension means having less available for expenses that feel more urgent today.
High housing costs, saving for a deposit and wider cost-of-living pressures can all compete with retirement contributions. Penfold said younger people also tend to favour savings options that are easier to access, including cash savings and ISAs.
Analysis from JPMorgan Asset Management has similarly found that Gen Z investors often prioritise ISAs over pensions because of their accessibility and flexibility.
The attraction is understandable. Money held in an ISA can generally be accessed before retirement, while pension savings are designed for the longer term.
That creates a particular problem for younger workers. They may want the financial freedom to retire earlier, but the money needed to make that possible has to compete with financial goals that are much closer.
Penfold co-founder Chris Eastwood reportedly said pension planning often asks Gen Z to prioritise a future that is decades away while they are dealing with rent, home saving and the rising cost of living.
“Many younger people already know financial security is important and aspire to achieve greater financial freedom, including earlier retirement than previous generations,” Eastwood reportedly said.
He argued that pensions need to be made simpler and more closely connected to the financial goals younger people are already working towards.
Could seeing the money change the way Gen Z saves?
One issue is visibility. A pension can feel distant when the only evidence of progress is an annual statement or a figure buried inside a provider's app.
Penfold has argued that technology could make it easier for younger workers to understand what they have saved and what their current contributions could mean later in life.
The planned pensions dashboards could play a role here. The UK system is designed to allow people to see information about their pensions, including their State Pension, in one place online. Pension schemes in scope are required to connect to the dashboards ecosystem by October 31, 2026.
That does not automatically mean people will save more. But having a clearer view of multiple pension pots could make retirement planning less abstract, particularly for younger workers who may change jobs several times during their careers.
The bigger challenge is therefore not simply getting Gen Z into pensions. Auto-enrolment has already made workplace pension saving much more common. The question is whether younger workers will increase their contributions as their incomes rise, rather than remain at the minimum level.
ForGen Z, retirement may still be decades away. But the amount saved in those early working years can have a long time to grow, making the decisions taken now increasingly important.

item.title: Egypt calls for end to Israeli violations, rejects forced displacement of Palestinians
item.description: Egypt's Prime Minister called for an end to Israeli violations and rejected forced displacement of Palestinians at the UN General Assembly.
item.content:encoded:
Egypt urged an end to Israeli violations against Palestinians on Friday, and firmly rejected any attempt to forcibly displace the population from the Gaza Strip or the occupied West Bank, including East Jerusalem, Anadolu reports.
Prime Minister Mostafa Madbouly told the 81st UN General Assembly in New York that the Gaza ceasefire must be fully implemented, Israeli violations halted and the withdrawal completed.
He called for a sustained humanitarian access, the start of early recovery and reconstruction, and a political process addressing the roots of the conflict.
“Peace cannot be built on uprooting a people from their land,” said Madbouly, warning that regional stability cannot be achieved while Palestinian suffering continues and the occupation is managed rather than ended.
He reaffirmed Egypt’s support for an independent, sovereign and geographically contiguous Palestinian state along the June 4, 1967, lines, with East Jerusalem as its capital.
READ: Egypt rejects annexation, displacement, calls for Palestinian state
Madbouly urged the international community to protect civilians, reject collective punishment and ensure respect for international humanitarian law.
Turning to regional security, he said no state could achieve security at the expense of its neighbors, through attacks on other countries or by threatening shipping, trade and energy routes.
He described Egypt’s water security as an “existential issue,” warning against unilateral measures on shared water resources and stressing the need for binding agreements under international law.
“Development by one party must not come at the expense of harm to others,” he said, adding that Egypt reserved its rights under international law to protect its water security.
Madbouly reaffirmed Cairo’s support for Sudan’s unity and state institutions amid the conflict.
He also renewed Egypt’s demand for comprehensive reform of the UN Security Council to address Africa’s underrepresentation and called for a Middle East free of nuclear weapons and other weapons of mass destruction.

item.title: Do Product Designers Need UI/UX Skills?
item.description: This article explains why UI/UX skills are essential for product designers, detailing the differences and overlaps between the two fields.
item.content:encoded:
Yes, and there isn't much room for debate here. Product design covers more ground than UI/UX design does on its own, but try doing the job without a working grasp of user experience and interface principles, and you'll run into trouble fast. A product can be backed by solid strategy and still fail if people find the interface confusing or the experience gets in their way.
Most product designers end up touching pretty much the whole lifecycle of a product at some point. One week they are spotting a user problem, the next they are running research, then it's wireframes, interface design, testing prototypes, and eventually sitting down with developers to figure out how the thing actually gets built. UI/UX skills show up at nearly every one of these stages, even when the job title never actually says "UI/UX" on it.
The more useful question isn't whether UI/UX matters. It's how much of it a given role actually requires, and whether product design and UI/UX design are really two names for the same job. That depends on the company. What tends to hold regardless is that designers with a foundation in both areas are better equipped to judge a product from the user's side of the screen, not just from how it looks in a file.
What Is Product Design?
Product design is mainly about building something that is able to solve a real user problem while still making sense for the business behind it. The process moves through several stages usually, though in practice these overlap way more than any list would suggest:
● Identifying what users actually need
● Researching to confirm it
● Framing the problem in usable terms
● Mapping how users move through the product
● Building wireframes
● Developing prototypes
● Designing the interface
● Testing whether the solution holds up
● Working with developers to ship it
● Adjusting based on what comes back
Visual design shows up fairly late in that list. A lot of the actual work happens before anyone opens a design tool.
What Is UI/UX Design?
UI is User Interface – what you see on the screen. The layout, the colours, the fonts, the buttons, how much space sits between things. If you can look at it or tap it, it's UI.
UX is User Experience – what happens once you start using the thing. Can you get where you're going without swearing at your phone? Where do people get stuck, or just close the app? UX designers spend their time on exactly that. They talk to real users, sketch out flows, build rough prototypes, run tests, and keep accessibility in mind so nobody gets left out.
Put simply, UI is how it looks and UX is whether it works. A beautiful app that nobody can figure out will still fail.
Is Product Design the Same as UI/UX?
Not quite, though the overlap is real enough that the confusion makes sense.
| | Product Design | UI/UX Design | | --- | --- | --- | | Scope | Strategy, research, UI, UX, business goals | Interface and experience | | Business involvement | Usually significant | Often narrower | | Typical work | Research, wireframes, prototypes, testing, developer collaboration | Wireframes, flows, visuals, testing | | Role structure | Can span the entire product lifecycle | Usually a defined function on a larger team |
Product design tends to be the wider category, with UI/UX sitting inside it as a more focused specialty. But job descriptions vary a lot in practice. Some companies expect one person to handle UI, UX, research, and strategy together. Others split those across separate roles entirely. Either way, UI/UX competency doesn't stop mattering just because it isn't the whole job.
Why Do Product Designers Need UI/UX Skills?
1. They lead to a more accurate read on user behaviour Looking good isn't enough on its own. If users are dropping off during checkout, the reason is often something other than the visuals — too many steps, unclear copy, a workflow that doesn't match how people actually think. UX research is what pushes a designer to find the real cause instead of guessing and redesigning the wrong thing.
2. They're what turns an idea into something usable Once a problem is understood, it has to be shown, not just described. That takes an understanding of hierarchy, layout, and typography — not for decoration, but so the resulting screen tells someone what to do without making them stop and think about it.
3. They keep product decisions grounded Product designers make calls on features, flows, and interactions constantly. UX principles give those calls something to be measured against: does this solve an actual problem, can people find it, what happens when someone gets it wrong. Skip this step and it's easy to ship something that made perfect sense in a meeting and confuses everyone who touches it afterward.
4. They make working across teams considerably easier Product designers rarely operate alone. They're explaining choices to engineers, product managers, researchers, whoever happens to be in the room that day. Being able to point to something concrete — an accessibility issue, a broken flow at a specific step — carries more weight than a vague preference, and it tends to move conversations forward faster.
Which UI/UX Skills Should Product Designers Learn?
Nobody needs to specialise in every corner of UI/UX. A handful of skills, though, come up again and again:
● User research, through interviews, surveys, or direct observation
● Wireframing, to establish structure before visual detail gets added
● Prototyping, to test an idea before development time gets spent on it
● Information architecture, so content and features stay easy to find
● Interaction design, covering how elements respond when someone actually uses them
● Visual design, meaning typography, colour, spacing, and consistency
● Usability testing, to catch problems by watching real people struggle or not
● Accessibility, so the product works for people who don't use it the way its designers do
Anyone building this foundation from the ground up might start with a structured UI UX Course, which walks through research, wireframing, prototyping, and interface design in a fairly guided way. Once that's in place, Simplilearn's broader product design courses go further into strategy and product thinking for anyone aiming at the full role rather than just the interface side of it.
Top 3 Product Design Courses from Simplilearn
1. Advanced Certification in UI/UX Design with Generative AI Offered with IIIT Bangalore, this runs about five months. You go through research, wireframing, prototyping, usability testing, and how AI fits into the design process. If your UI/UX basics still feel shaky, this is a sensible place to begin.
2. AI-Powered Professional Certification in Product Management This one is delivered with SP Jain School of Global Management and leans toward strategy, roadmaps, and making decisions with AI in the mix. The case studies come from companies like Netflix and Instagram.
3. Professional Certificate Programme in AI Product Development & Innovation Designed and delivered by IIM Kozhikode, this program follows AI-driven products from the first idea all the way to launch. There's also a prompt engineering module that ties into real product planning work.
Do Product Designers Need to Be Experts in UI and UX?
Not really. It comes down to where you end up working. A large company usually has its own UX researchers and UI designers, sometimes an accessibility specialist too, so the product designer spends the day keeping all of them moving together. A small startup is different. There, one person often covers the lot, and the first few months tend to be messy. Nobody is asking for mastery of every corner. What teams want is someone who notices how a tiny UI change, like shifting a button, can throw off the whole product.
Can a UI/UX Designer Become a Product Designer?
Yes, and plenty of people have made exactly that move. A UI/UX background is a strong head start, because researching users, building prototypes and spotting a confusing flow quickly are things that take years to get good at. What's usually missing is the business side. That means tying a design problem to what the company is actually after, making sense of the numbers, choosing what to leave out, and standing firm in a room where engineers and stakeholders see things differently. The skills carry over; they just need to stretch further.
Final Verdict: Do Product Designers Need UI/UX Skills?
Yes, and putting them off is a mistake. Product design reaches well beyond UI/UX, but UI/UX is the part that keeps everything else standing. Start with the fundamentals and add strategy once they feel solid. People who try to learn both at once often end up decent at each and strong at neither.

TORM plc is an international product tanker company that transports refined oil products and other energy-related cargoes by sea. Its vessels carry products such as gasoline, jet fuel, diesel and other clean petroleum products between production, storage and consumption markets.

item.title: Ticket no. TL 360615. wins ₹30 crore first prize of Keralam government’s Thiruvonam bumper lottery
item.description: Ticket number TL 360615 won the 30 crore rupee first prize in the Kerala government's Thiruvonam bumper lottery.
item.content:encoded:
Ticket no. TL 360615. wins ₹30 crore first prize of Keralam government’s Thiruvonam bumper lottery
The Thiruvonam Bumper Lottery, priced at ₹500 per ticket, had seen record sales this year
The ₹30 crore first prize of the 2026 Thiruvonam bumper lottery operated by the Keralam government’s State Lotteries Directorate went to ticket number TL 360615.
The prize-winning ticket was sold by lottery agent Aneesh M.V. of Kannur (Agency no. C-3789).
The Thiruvonam Bumper Lottery, priced at ₹500 per ticket, had seen record sales this year. All 90 lakh tickets printed by the Kerala State Lotteries Directorate were fully sold out, Lotteries Director K.S. Anju said on Friday (September 25, 2026).
Health Minister K. Muraleedharan inaugurated the draw held at Gorky Bhavan in Thiruvananthapuram on Saturday (September 26, 2026). Trial runs were held before the actual draw.
The total prize money under this lottery amount to र125.56 crore.
The other prizes are as follows: Second prize (र1 crore each to 20 winners), third prize (र25 lakh to 20 winners - two in each series), fourth prize (र5 lakh to 10 winners - one per series), fifth prize (र2 lakh each to 10 winners - one per series), sixth prize (र5000 to 54,000 winners), seventh prize (र2000 to 81,000 winners), eighth prize - र1000 to 1,24,000 winners), ninth prize (र500 to 2,75,400 winners), consolation prize (र5 lakh each to nine winners).
Once the winner is identified, the Lotteries Directorate will transfer the prize money into the winner’s bank account after deducting the agent’s commission and tax. The winner/winners will also have to remit surcharge and cess on the winnings.
The Lotteries Directorate has hiked the first prize amount from ₹25 crore to ₹30 crore this year. This lottery carries the highest prize money offered by the government-run Kerala State Lotteries in its history. Although a major chunk of the revenue from lottery sales goes into the prize money, the State Lotteries remain a major revenue source for the State government.
Chief Minister V.D. Satheesan had launched this year’s Thiruvonam Bumper Lottery in July. Sales began on July 20.
On Saturday (September 26, 2026), Mr. Muraleedharan also launched the 2026 Pooja Bumper Lottery, which carries a first prize of र12 crore.

item.title: America is free. Washington should not be up for sale
item.description: A Congresswoman advocates for legislation to curb corruption and self-enrichment among politicians in Washington.
item.content:encoded:
'As Americans stretch every dollar, career politicians in Washington have only gotten richer at our expense.'
George Washington once said, “Few men have virtue to withstand the highest bidder. ” And while much has happened in the nearly 250 years since he made this sharp observation, human nature has remained the same.
The headlines are endless and endlessly colorful. Bribes paid in gold bars and cash crammed into coat pockets. Donor money spent on designer goods. Politicians trading stocks with insider information, using taxpayer dollars to line their own pockets.
Corruption is a tale as old as time, but when investment funds built to copy stock trades of members of Congress consistently outperform the S&P 500, you know you’ve got a problem. Washington needs to be held accountable. Self-dealing has become all too common, and as Americans stretch every dollar to afford groceries, gas, housing, and health care, career politicians in Washington have only gotten richer at our expense.
That’s because for decades these very politicians have neglected to address the kitchen-table issues that matter most to Americans’ daily lives. In the words of President Washington, they have sold the American people’s best interests away to the “highest bidder,” trading stocks, cozying up with special interest groups, and appropriating millions of federal dollars wherever their own personal financial interests lie. I ran for Congress to break the gridlock in Washington, D.C.
, and deliver real results for California families—and I did. When Congress took up the largest tax reform in years, I was the only Californian negotiating with Speaker Mike Johnson and President Donald Trump to increase the State and Local Tax Deduction by 300 percent so hardworking families can keep more of their hard-earned money. I’ve worked to lower health care costs, cut middle-class taxes, protect our seniors, and support small businesses across Southern California.
Now, I’m fighting to hold Washington accountable, so we can keep getting things done for the American people. I’m supporting legislation like the Stop Insider Trading Act, which passed the House of Representatives in July, and the Restore Trust in Congress Act to ban members of Congress from trading individual stocks. I recently cosponsored the Congressional Pension Accountability Act and End Government Pensions for Sexual Abusers Act to strip disgraced politicians of their taxpayer-funded pensions when they violate public trust.
I also support term limits for members of Congress, because career politicians should not be camped out in D.C. for decades, sinking into the swamp, cashing in year over year, and forgetting who they represent. Unfortunately, there are as many ways for politicians to game the system as there are special interest groups on K Street.
While I was thrilled to help advance the Stop Insider Trading Act out of the House, that must be the first step in accountability, not the last. Last week, I introduced the Stop Congressional Self-Enrichment Resolution to bar members of Congress from appropriating federal dollars for projects that increase their own personal net worth. Under current House rules, members must certify that they do not have direct financial conflicts of interest when they request Community Project Funding , or earmarks.
Where this rule misses the mark is that indirect financial interests can factor just as heavily into whether an elected official makes millions when bringing federal dollars back home. For example, a member could request an earmark for a nonprofit where their spouse serves on the board or fund a new park next to an apartment building they own, increasing the property’s value and ultimately boosting their own bottom line.
My resolution sets a stronger standard by making clear that members should not in any way, directly or indirectly, benefit financially from taxpayer-funded earmarks. This resolution and others I’ve supported are about more than just closing a loophole. Self-enrichment and corruption in Congress go against every fiber of what our Founding Fathers envisioned for this country. Our Constitution is a masterpiece that calls on leaders from every corner of the nation to represent America’s many unique voices.
When politicians exploit their positions to benefit themselves, they not only betray the public’s trust; they silence the very voices they were sent here to represent. We can, and must, do better. I’ll keep working to root out corruption wherever I see it and ensure Congress is working to lower costs, rein in health care prices, and have your best interests at heart.
Congresswoman Young Kim represents California’s 40th District and chairs the House Foreign Affairs Subcommittee on East Asia and the Pacific. She also serves on the House Financial Services Committee and the Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party. The views expressed in this article are the writer's own.
